messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi remembers the silence more than the explosion. He was just twenty, a newly qualified doctor on his first humanitarian tour, suturing a child’s arm in the relative quiet of the field clinic. The world vanished in a roar of pressure and heat, a deafening blast that threw him against a supply cabinet. But what followed was worse. A thick, ringing silence, absolute and profound, filled only by the taste of dust and the sudden, desperate struggle for air in his lungs. He remembers that feeling of suffocation, the frantic gasping in the chalky darkness, more than the chaos that came after. That silence, and the fight for breath, became the anchors of what happened that day.

Six months later, back in the United States and starting a residency, the event has refused to settle into a coherent past. Kofi’s memory of the attack is a collection of broken shards. He sees the colour of the tent canvas just before it ripped apart, feels the sharp pain in his shoulder, hears a single, high-pitched scream. But there is no narrative, no sequence. These fragmented pieces float untethered, and great black voids separate them, parts of the event he simply cannot recall no matter how hard he tries. When a fragment does break through, it brings with it a wave of conviction: the world is not a place of order and healing, but of random, brutal chaos. The attack completely shattered his belief in a predictable, safe world, a belief that had been the very foundation of his desire to become a doctor. This profound loss of faith is reinforced every time a memory surfaces; the disjointed images serve as proof that nothing makes sense anymore.

The memory fragments themselves have become their own source of terror. The mental image of the swirling dust cloud is enough to make his chest tighten, his breathing shallow, a physical echo of the suffocation he felt in the collapsed tent. This somatic trigger often comes without warning, a ghost of the past re-enacting itself on his body. He has also found himself pushing the memories away before they can fully form. The moment he feels a coherent thought about the attack begin to surface, a powerful, instinctual 'no' rises up, a mental wall that slams down to protect him from what he might see. He has come to believe that he is no longer the same person who went overseas, and this sense of a fractured identity makes the past a forbidden territory. He is afraid that fully remembering would only confirm how broken he is, so he fights to keep the memory in pieces, which in turn perpetuates its power over him.

This new, terrifying belief system—that he is irrevocably changed and that danger is everywhere—has made him hypervigilant. He scans every room he enters, sits with his back to the wall, and lives in a state of constant, low-grade alert. This need to be on guard all the time means he is acutely attuned to the very things that now torment him. Last week, while doing rounds, the hospital’s backup generator failed, plunging the corridor into an abrupt, humming silence. For Kofi, it wasn't just a power cut; it was a signal of imminent danger, a direct replay of the moment before the screaming started. The thought was immediate and absolute: *I have to be ready.* The sudden quiet, which most people wouldn't even notice, now serves as a potent trigger, instantly activating his conviction that he is unsafe and must prepare for violence. His world has become a minefield of his own making, where his attempts to stay safe only make him more vulnerable to the echoes of the past.

Kofi decided to seek therapy after an incident in the emergency department. A multi-car pile-up brought in a wave of trauma patients, and in the controlled chaos of the ER, he found himself overwhelmed not by the work, but by the familiar sights and sounds of injury. A colleague clapped him on the shoulder to get his attention, and Kofi flinched so violently he nearly dropped a tray of instruments. He saw the concern in his attending physician's eyes and realised the chasm between the competent doctor he was supposed to be and the frightened man he had become was now visible to everyone. He feels like he doesn't know himself anymore, and his greatest fear is that the person he was—the one who believed in healing and order—is gone for good, lost in the dust and silence of a single afternoon.
